text: A 222-metre crater changed the Moon kilometres beyond its rim. The impact happened in 2024; the new research reveals its wider reach. And four other breakthroughs happened this week: wearable AI, electronic materials, cartilage biology, and fault experiments. From Earth, the Moon can look almost frozen in time. But a spacecraft watching the same ground for years can catch changes that a single photograph would miss. Researchers describe the McGetchin crater, named after lunar scientist Tom McGetchin. It formed in the spring of 2024 and measures about 222 metres across. The surprise lies outside its visible edge. Measurements from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter's Diviner instrument found a cooler region extending more than three kilometres from the impact. Diviner measures surface temperatures. Comparing observations before and after the collision helps researchers work out how the surrounding soil changed. Their interpretation is that material thrown out by the impact churned and loosened the fine lunar ground, known as regolith. That altered how it stores and releases heat. The temperature measurements are evidence of this disturbance; they are not a film of the collision itself. Impacts this large are statistically unusual, but a once-per-century estimate is not a timetable. Smaller impacts happen much more often. Why does this matter? The surface that future explorers will investigate is continually being reworked. Understanding that process helps scientists interpret lunar history and the distribution of material in the soil. A fresh crater also gives scientists a dated reference point for comparing how lunar terrain evolves over time. The practical lesson is also about observation: keep watching a familiar place, and an apparently quiet landscape can reveal a much bigger story.
